Look for the math

Interest added to interest grows faster than interest added once — and the more often it is added, the faster it grows.

Simple versus compound

At 12% a year, 1,000 borrowed for a year costs 1,120 with a single assessment. Assessed twice at 6%, it becomes 1000 × 1.06² = 1123.60: an effective rate of 12.36%. The page's table for 1, 2, 4 and 12 assessments gives 1120.00, 1123.60, 1125.50 and 1126.82 — the logic test reproduces all four.

Geometric series

With yearly rate q compounded m times, each deposit period multiplies the balance by 1 + q/m. After N periods that is a geometric series, giving P(1+q/m)^N + p((1+q/m)^N − 1)/(q/m) for savings. For a loan, the same series inverted gives the payment that clears the debt: P·r(1+r)^n / ((1+r)^n − 1) with r the rate per payment. The test checks both by simulating every payment and every deposit.

Set the interest to 0. What do the two formulas become then?
